title: Select, set out and maintain materials, tools and equipment

lessons.title: Selecting the right materials, tools and equipment
lessons.html:
Start with the job

Every task at a grain handling site needs the right materials, tools and equipment. Picking the wrong spanner, an unsuitable sampling spear or the wrong grade of grease wastes time, damages equipment and can cause injuries. As a supervisor or senior operator, you are expected to choose correctly and to show others how.

Read the job requirements

Before selecting anything, check the job card, work instruction, maintenance schedule or manufacturer's manual. Ask:

  • What exactly must be done, and to what standard?
  • What size, type and quantity of material is specified, for example bearing type, belt width, bolt size or lubricant grade?
  • Which tools and measuring instruments are required?
  • Is special equipment needed, such as a lifting device, a calibrated moisture meter or a gas detector?
  • Is a permit needed, such as a lockout, hot work or confined space permit?

Check what you select

Inspect each item before you take it to the job:

  • Hand tools: no cracked handles, mushroomed chisel heads or worn jaws.
  • Power tools: intact cords and plugs, guards fitted, test tag current where your site uses tags.
  • Measuring instruments: calibration date valid, zeroed, clean.
  • Materials: correct specification, within shelf life, undamaged packaging, food-grade lubricants where there is contact with grain.
  • PPE: suited to the hazard and in good condition.

Food safety and grain contact

Grain is food and feed. Anything that may touch it must not contaminate it. Use food-grade greases and oils on equipment that contacts grain, do not use glass in grain areas, and account for all small parts, such as nuts and split pins, so nothing ends up in the product stream.

Requesting from stores

Complete the stores requisition accurately with part numbers and quantities. Sign for what you receive and check it against the request. Report shortages early so that work is not delayed during intake season.

lessons.title: Setting out the work area
lessons.html:
Prepare before you start

Setting out means arranging the work area, materials and tools so the job can be done safely and efficiently. A well set out job is quicker, safer and leaves fewer loose items behind.

Make the area safe

  1. Confirm the equipment is isolated and locked out according to your site lockout procedure. Test that it cannot start before anyone works on it.
  2. Barricade the area and place warning signs so that forklifts, trucks and other workers keep clear.
  3. Check for dust build-up. Grain dust is combustible. Clean it away before grinding, welding or any work that can cause sparks, and obtain a hot work permit where required.
  4. Make sure there is adequate lighting and ventilation.
  5. Check the escape route and the position of the nearest fire extinguisher and first aid kit.

Arrange materials and tools

  • Place tools within easy reach on a mat, tray or toolbox, not on the floor or on top of machines where they can fall into hoppers.
  • Keep materials in the order they will be used.
  • Keep heavy items low and stable. Use correct lifting technique or lifting aids.
  • Keep cables and hoses out of walkways or covered.
  • Keep chemicals, such as solvents and lubricants, in labelled containers with drip trays.

Brief the team

Before starting, hold a short toolbox talk. Explain the task, the hazards, who does what and the sequence of work. Confirm everyone has the right PPE. Agree how the team will communicate around noisy equipment.

Count tools in and out

At grain sites, a tool left inside an elevator boot, conveyor or bin can damage equipment or end up in the grain. Use a tool list or shadow board. Count tools at the start and again before the equipment is released.

lessons.title: Maintaining and storing tools and equipment
lessons.html:
Look after what you use

Tools and equipment are expensive. Good care extends their life and keeps them safe and accurate. Poor care leads to breakdowns in the middle of harvest, when the site can least afford it.

After the job

  1. Count and collect all tools and leftover materials.
  2. Clean tools of grain dust, grease and dirt.
  3. Inspect for damage and wear. Tag and remove damaged tools from service, and report them.
  4. Return unused materials to stores and record what was used.
  5. Dispose of waste correctly: used oil and rags into marked containers, scrap metal to the scrap area.
  6. Remove barricades, close the permit and release the equipment through the lockout procedure only when all people and tools are clear.

Routine maintenance

ItemTypical care
Hand toolsClean, oil to prevent rust, sharpen or replace worn parts
Power toolsInspect cords and guards, clean vents, service as per manual
Measuring instrumentsStore in cases, check against standards, send for calibration on schedule
Sampling equipmentClean between lots, check for bent spears or blocked openings

Storage

Store tools in a dry, secure place, each in its own position. Shadow boards make missing tools obvious. Store materials according to the supplier instructions: some must be kept cool, dry or away from sunlight. Rotate stock so older items are used first.

Records

Keep a register of tools and equipment, calibration certificates and maintenance done. Record faults and repairs. These records support audits and help plan replacement budgets.

Key points

  • Select materials and tools from the job requirements and inspect them before use.
  • Use food-grade lubricants and control loose parts where equipment contacts grain.
  • Isolate and lock out equipment, clean away dust and barricade before work.
  • Count tools in and out so nothing is left in machines or grain.
  • Clean, inspect, store and record tools after every job.

quiz.question: Where should you first look to find out which materials a job needs?

options.text: The job card, work instruction or manufacturer's manual
Use whatever is in the toolbox

quiz.question: What type of lubricant should be used on equipment that contacts grain?
Why should dust be cleaned away before grinding or welding?

options.text: Grain dust is combustible and sparks can ignite it
It is only required in winter

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of counting tools in and out?

options.text: To make the job last longer
To make sure no tool is left inside machines or grain
To reduce the number of tools bought

quiz.question: What should you do with a damaged tool found after a job?

options.text: Put it back on the shadow board
Tag it, remove it from service and report it
Give it to a new worker

quiz.question: Equipment may be released from lockout only when all people and tools are clear.
A measuring instrument with an expired calibration date is fine to use if it looks clean.
Which steps are part of setting out a work area safely? (select all that apply)

Barricade the area and place warning signs
Place tools on top of the hopper for easy reach
